look_here_first: VASEYGRASS: a coarse tall grass with MANY thin one-sided spreading or drooping racemes along an elongated seedhead axis (often 10–20, overlapping other taxa). To separate from dallisgrass, measure mature spikelets: vaseygrass mostly 2–3 mm with silky margins, dallisgrass mostly 3–4 mm. Its existing photo shows numerous racemes, but neither a scale nor confirmed glume hairs.

crew_field_steps: Trace the single central flowerhead axis and the many narrow racemes spreading in different directions; the installed photo shows this architecture clearly.
Recognize that each slender raceme carries rows of tiny spikelets along one side; the individual hairs are not resolvable in the wide view.
Collect base/ligule, a measured spikelet and the FULL head to distinguish dallisgrass; a distant photograph alone is only a vaseygrass candidate.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole rooted bunch, height context, basal sheaths.
One ENTIRE panicle with every raceme attachment visible.
Macro of pairwise spikelets next to millimeter scale and silky margin hairs.
True membranous ligule at blade/sheath junction; compare dallisgrass.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Count branches on ONE complete culm, not overlapping heads. Contrast 2–3 mm spikelets under measured macro with 3–4 mm long-haired dallisgrass; do not key solely by abundance of racemes or overall height. Use Florida paspalum as another few-branch, large-spikelet look-alike.
do_not_use_alone: Number of racemes without the entire flowering axis
Habitat, height, or vegetative tuft in isolation
Microscopic glume hairs or spikelet length inferred from a photo without scale
comparisons.field_identification_note: Record full head with branch count and centimeter ruler; 5 mature spikelets face-on and on edge with millimeter scale; compare lower/upper glumes and silky hair margin. Same-plant rooted tuft and true collar still needed.

visual_comparison.title: Paspalum urvillei — photographed field ID and look-alikes
visual_comparison.subtitle: Photos already in the Hays library, inspected individually. Annotations point ONLY to visible shapes/parts; small hairs/glumes and exact species determinations await specimen proof.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: COUNT COMPLETE RACEMES → MEASURE 5 RIPE SPIKELETS → CHECK MARGINAL HAIRS → ROOTED BASE/COLLAR. DALLIS few large silky; VASEY many small silky; FLORIDA few big round; PUBIFLORUM smaller oval; SETACEUM narrow variable; DISTICHUM two + real stolons.

items.caption: This is Paspalum dilatatum according to its existing source photo, NOT Paspalum urvillei. Compare the pictured flowering architecture or plant habit; different frames are not measured side-by-side specimens.
items.why_it_matters: Vaseygrass tends to be taller with more racemes (commonly 10–20) and small roughly 2–3 mm hairy spikelets; dallisgrass usually bears fewer racemes and bigger 3–4 mm silky-edged spikelets. Florida paspalum generally has fewer racemes and large broad spikelets. Johnson grass has an open branching PANICLE rather than the flat, one-sided raceme rows typical of Paspalum.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Paspalum: what to inspect
steps: Record full head with branch count and centimeter ruler; 5 mature spikelets face-on and on edge with millimeter scale; compare lower/upper glumes and silky hair margin. Same-plant rooted tuft and true collar still needed.
First show the WHOLE head, then ONE one-sided raceme and attached spikelets. Never treat a photograph of one branch as total raceme count.
Obtain a real intact mature spikelet and measure it with 1-mm reference; use margin hair pattern and glumes to separate close Paspalum taxa.
Photograph blade/sheath joint and same-plant rootstock; knotgrass needs actually rooted horizontal stolons, not merely a low mat.
If plant photo is source-labelled only, keep identity tentative and leave existing county-native fields unchanged.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Vaseygrass tends to be taller with more racemes (commonly 10–20) and small roughly 2–3 mm hairy spikelets; dallisgrass usually bears fewer racemes and bigger 3–4 mm silky-edged spikelets. Florida paspalum generally has fewer racemes and large broad spikelets. Johnson grass has an open branching PANICLE rather than the flat, one-sided raceme rows typical of Paspalum.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Gross photo structures are references, NOT expert confirmation. Even new licensed images are PROVISIONAL — USER PHOTO REVIEW PENDING and not proof of Hays County presence.
